question: What documents must international travelers present when entering Uganda?
answer: Under URA customs and immigration guidelines at https://ura.go.ug/en/documents-at-the-point-of-entry/: 1) Valid passport with at least six months validity remaining from entry date; 2) Valid Ugandan visa (electronic e-Visa or visa-free entry for eligible nationalities); 3) Yellow Fever Vaccination Certificate (mandatory for all travelers over one year of age); 4) Proof of onward or return travel ticket; 5) Passenger Baggage Declaration for goods exceeding the USD 500/2,000 personal allowance.

question: What documents are needed for a foreign company to register and operate in Uganda?
answer: A foreign corporate entity entering Uganda requires: 1) Certificate of Incorporation from home country; 2) Board resolution authorizing registration of a foreign branch/subsidiary in Uganda; 3) Certified Memorandum and Articles of Association; 4) Certified list of company directors and company secretary (names, nationalities, addresses); 5) Official registered local physical office address in Uganda; 6) Recent audited financial statements certified by an auditor; 7) URA Tax Identification Number (TIN); 8) Municipal Trading License from KCCA or local authority; 9) Uganda Investment Authority (UIA) Investment License where applicable.

question: Which documents are required at the point of entry for goods?
answer: Under URA guidelines at https://ura.go.ug/en/documents-at-the-point-of-entry/, ten (10) primary documents are required: 1) Bill of Lading (B/L) or Airway Bill (AWB) — legal contract of carriage, cargo receipt, and document of title; 2) Marine/Cargo Insurance Certificate — covers loss or damage in transit; 3) Proforma Invoice — quotation format used for import licensing and letters of credit; 4) Commercial Invoice — definitive transaction invoice used by customs to assess import duty and VAT; 5) Certificate of Origin — proves country of manufacture for preferential tariffs (EAC, COMESA); 6) Permits for Restricted Goods — ministerial licenses under the External Trade Act (Cap. 88); 7) Purchase Order — binding commercial purchase agreement; 8) Packing List — itemizes contents, package dimensions, and gross/net weights; 9) Sales Contract — sets terms of delivery (Incoterms) and payment obligations; 10) Evidence of Payment — verified bank swift transfer slips, drafts, or statements.

question: Why is a Certificate of Origin mandatory at the point of entry?
answer: A Certificate of Origin is required by customs authorities to verify the exact manufacturing origin of imported goods, determining whether the consignment qualifies for zero or preferential duty rates under regional trade protocols (such as the East African Community Customs Union or COMESA rules of origin) or standard Common External Tariff (CET) rates.

question: What is the statutory basis for restricted goods permits at the point of entry?
answer: Permits for restricted goods are issued under Sections 3 and 4 of the External Trade Act (Cap. 88) by the Minister of Trade, Industry and Cooperatives. Regulated items (such as used tyres, communication equipment, firearms, chemicals, or food products) cannot be cleared through customs without the requisite ministerial permit.
